hook.line: A shaken tourist on the Séptima asks Tomás how to get to the police station, and Tomás wants to answer with more than a wave of the hand. Naming the road you travel along takes one small word.
hook.es: Siga por la Séptima hasta la calle 72.
hook.en: Carry on along Seventh Avenue to 72nd Street. (formal)

rule:
English names a road with *along*, *down*, *up* or *on*. Spanish uses one small word for all of them: *por*.

The verb gives the direction, and *por* names the road:
*seguir por*: carry on along
*subir por*: go up
*bajar por*: go down
*caminar por*, *manejar por*, *ir por*: walk, drive, go along

Don't drop *por*. *Siga la Séptima* sounds like following a person named Séptima. *Por* also picks the side: *por la derecha*.

For a fixed spot, not a route, use *en*: *Estoy en la Séptima.*
smallPrint: Teachers call this *por* of route, or *por* of path: it marks the space you move through, not where you end up (that's *a* or *hasta*).

pitfalls.wrong: Siga la Séptima hasta la calle 72.
pitfalls.right: Siga por la Séptima hasta la calle 72.
pitfalls.why: Almost. English drops the little word (*carry on Seventh*), but Spanish needs *por* to name the road.

pitfalls.wrong: Iba en la Caracas cuando pasó.
pitfalls.right: Iba por la Caracas cuando pasó.
pitfalls.why: Almost. *En* is for a fixed spot; when you are moving along a road, Spanish uses *por*.

pitfalls.wrong: En Colombia se maneja en la derecha.
pitfalls.right: En Colombia se maneja por la derecha.
pitfalls.why: Almost. English says *on the right*, but the side you travel on takes *por* in Spanish.

personal: Think of your usual walk or drive to work, school or the shop. Say it in two or three short sentences with *por* (*Camino por…*, *Subo por…*).
